pages.title: The whole design, end to end
pages.for: Design the submain first, then each long or heavily loaded circuit, and carry every result forward. The far end inherits everything upstream: the supply, the submain and the circuit. Check it against every length, every drop from the intake, the device's maximum Zs, the heat in the cpc and breaking capacity.
pages.rule:
Length = plan length + every vertical run
Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, with It ≥ In ÷ the factors
Total drop = submain drop (÷ √3 onto a single-phase circuit) + circuit drop
Zs at the end = Zs at the board + circuit R1+R2
R1+R2 = mΩ/m × multiplier × length ÷ 1000
cpc or armour: S = √(I² × t) ÷ k, with I = 230 × 1.1 ÷ Zs
Icn ≥ the fault level at the device

Read t from the device's curve. An MCB tripping instantly clears within 0.1 s.
Lighting may drop 3%: 6.90 V single-phase, 12 V three-phase.
Other circuits may drop 5%: 11.50 V single-phase, 20 V three-phase.
A light load usually runs out of Zs first. A heavy load usually runs out of voltage first.
Check the cpc's heat at both ends.

traps.text: Using the plan length without the runs up and down at each end.
Starting a circuit's Zs from Ze instead of Zs at its board.
Adding a three-phase submain's drop to a single-phase circuit without dividing by √3.
traps.cite: Guide p.6; formula sheet step 7 note

traps.text: Checking only the longest circuit when a shorter one carries more current.
Checking the cpc's heat only at the far end, where the fault current is smallest.
traps.cite: IET EngX forum on the adiabatic check, in research (contested)

pages.where: BS 7671 Appendix 4 for It and mV/A/m. Table 41.3 for maximum Zs. Tables 43.1 and 54.2 to 54.4 for k. The maker's data for armour resistance and Icn.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A lighting circuit runs from a sub-board. Ze at the origin is 0.10 Ω. The submain's R1+R2 is 0.30 Ω. The circuit's own R1+R2 is 0.50 Ω. What is Zs at the far end of the circuit?
pages.answer: 0.90 Ω: Ze + the submain + the circuit
pages.alt: Zs at the sub-board = 0.10 + 0.30 = 0.40 Ω Zs at the far end = 0.40 + 0.50 = 0.90 Ω A fault at the far end drives current back through every cable to the supply, so every one of them is in the loop. 0.60 Ω leaves out the submain. 0.80 Ω leaves out Ze.
options: 0.90 Ω: Ze + the submain + the circuit
pages.html:
Zs at the sub-board = 0.10 + 0.30 = 0.40 Ω

Zs at the far end = 0.40 + 0.50 = 0.90 Ω

A fault at the far end drives current back through every cable to the supply, so every one of them is in the loop.

0.60 Ω leaves out the submain. 0.80 Ω leaves out Ze.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text:
The design ends at the last luminaire, but it starts at the intake. A fault at the far end flows back through the circuit, the submain and the supply. The voltage drops along all of them too. So every check at the far end carries everything upstream with it.

Design the submain first, then the circuit, and carry each result forward.
pages.alt: The design ends at the last luminaire, but it starts at the intake. A fault at the far end flows back through the circuit, the submain and the supply. The voltage drops along all of them too. So every check at the far end carries everything upstream with it. Design the submain first, then the circuit, and carry each result forward. BEFORE YOU CALL THE DESIGN DONE Every length of the run, not just the route on plan. Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz for each cable. Every voltage drop from the intake to the end. A three-phase drop turned into its single-phase share. Zs at the end against the device's maximum.
pages.html:
The design ends at the last luminaire, but it starts at the intake. A fault at the far end flows back through the circuit, the submain and the supply. The voltage drops along all of them too. So every check at the far end carries everything upstream with it.

Design the submain first, then the circuit, and carry each result forward.

Before you call the design done

  • Every length of the run, not just the route on plan.
  • Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz for each cable.
  • Every voltage drop from the intake to the end.
  • A three-phase drop turned into its single-phase share.
  • Zs at the end against the device's maximum.
  • The thermal constraints, with SWA armour as the cpc justified by calculation.
  • Breaking capacity at each device.
If it is skipped: Leave out a length or the submain and the far end looks better on paper than it will measure. The breaker may not open in time.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: At 1.21 A the Zs bar is the first to cross its line, near 104.5 m. At 4.89 A the drop bar crosses first, near 38.9 m. At 45.0 m and 4.89 A the drop is 7.82 V, past its line. Zs is 1.794 Ω, still inside.
pages.alt: MDB Submain Board Supply Circuit Far end At the far end of the circuit Voltage drop from the intake past its line 6.90 V limit First to its line: 38.9 m Zs at the far end inside its line 3.64 Ω maximum Reaches its line: 104.5 m What the board hands on The circuit's own Drop from the intake 7.82 V Zs at the far end 1.794 Ω The drop bar is past 6.90 V, so the far end gets too little voltage. The Zs bar is still inside its line. At 4.89 A, the voltage runs out first. Each metre of the circuit adds to both bars. It adds 31 mV for every amp it carries, so the drop grows with the load.
pages.html:
Drop from the intake7.82 V
Zs at the far end1.794 Ω

The drop bar is past 6.90 V, so the far end gets too little voltage. The Zs bar is still inside its line. At 4.89 A, the voltage runs out first.

Each metre of the circuit adds to both bars. It adds 31 mV for every amp it carries, so the drop grows with the load. It adds 24.2 × 1.28 = 30.976 mΩ to the fault loop, whatever the load. The load in service makes no difference to Zs.

So on this board a light load runs out of Zs first. A heavy one runs out of voltage first. Both start from what the board hands on.

The longest circuit is not always the worst. Check every long or heavily loaded circuit against both limits.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A three-phase submain drops 6.00 V. A single-phase lighting circuit from its board drops 4.00 V. The supply is 230 V single-phase and 400 V three-phase. Does the lighting circuit meet its voltage drop limit?
pages.why: The submain's 6.00 V is the drop between lines. A single-phase circuit sees only the line-to-neutral part: 6.00 ÷ √3 = 3.46 V. Add the circuit's 4.00 V: 7.46 V. Lighting is allowed 3% of 230 V, 6.90 V. So it fails.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: The submain runs 20.0 m with its vertical runs. It needs an It of 11.63 A. The 4 mm² cable carries 44 A. It drops 1.64 V, which is 0.95 V on a single-phase circuit.
pages.alt: Assume the submain is four-core 4 mm² 90 °C thermosetting SWA cable, alone on a perforated tray in the ceiling void. A 10 A type C breaker at the MDB protects it. Both are practice choices. The lighting currents rest on assumed power factors. The route is 17.0 m on plan. Take 1.5 m at each end for the runs up into the ceiling void and down to the board. Measure those on a real job. THE DBL2 SUBMAIN Length = 17.0 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 20.0 m Ib is the heaviest phase, L1: 8.22 A. In is 10 A, so Ib ≤ In. Take the third harmonic as 20% here.
pages.html:
Assume the submain is four-core 4 mm² 90 °C thermosetting SWA cable, alone on a perforated tray in the ceiling void. A 10 A type C breaker at the MDB protects it. Both are practice choices. The lighting currents rest on assumed power factors.

The route is 17.0 m on plan. Take 1.5 m at each end for the runs up into the ceiling void and down to the board. Measure those on a real job.

The DBL2 submain

Length = 17.0 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 20.0 m

Ib is the heaviest phase, L1: 8.22 A. In is 10 A, so Ib ≤ In.

Take the third harmonic as 20% here. At that level, size the cable on the line current, with the 0.86 factor from Table 4Aa.

The building is at 20 °C. Take Ca as 1.00 anyway and claim nothing for the cooler air. Cg is 1, because the cable is alone on its tray. Ci is 1.

It ≥ 10 ÷ (1.00 × 1 × 1 × 0.86) = 11.63 A

Table 4E4A, Method E, three loaded cores: 4 mm² carries 44 A.

Iz = 44 × 0.86 = 37.84 A, so 8.22 ≤ 10 ≤ 37.84.

Voltage drop = 10 × 8.22 × 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.64 V, three-phase.

Its share on a single-phase circuit = 1.64 ÷ √3 = 0.95 V.

Smaller sizes pass too. 4 mm² is kept for its armour, checked next. The 20% harmonic puts current in the neutral. So some designers work the submain one phase at a time, with the two-core 12 mV/A/m. That gives 1.97 V. It is already a single-phase drop, so add it to the circuit's drop as it is, with no ÷ √3. Either way it is far inside the limit.

pages.html:
Your showroom: the supply and DBL2Scenario

A newly built car showroom, on a 230/400 V three-phase four-wire TN-C-S supply. Ze is 0.1 Ω and the prospective fault current is 4.6 kA. The building is at 20 °C. A four-core SWA submain runs from the MDB in the plant room to DBL2, the lighting board in the tools and warranty store. DBL2's circuits include C7, for the foyer lights and the walkway bollards.

Submain: 17.0 m on plan + 1.5 m up + 1.5 m down = 20.0 m

Carried forward
(b)DBL2's lighting: current on L18.22 A
(e)DBL2's submain: design load, after Table 4Aa's factor9.56 A
(f)DBL2 submain: least armour area, on the plan length5.00 mm²

From the worked example: the submain runs 20.0 m with its vertical runs. It drops 1.64 V three-phase, which is 0.95 V on a single-phase circuit. It is four-core 4 mm² SWA on a 10 A type C breaker, and its armour is the cpc.

Each core is 4.61 mΩ/m and the armour is 6.8 mΩ/m, both at 20 °C. Use the 1.28 multiplier on both.

R1+R2 = (4.61 + 6.8) × 1.28 × 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.292 Ω

Zs at DBL2 = 0.1 + 0.292 = 0.392 Ω

0.392 Ω is far under the 10 A type C's 2.19 Ω. The least fault current is 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.392 = 557.40 A. That is well past 100 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s.

Now re-check the armour. The greatest fault current at DBL2 is 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.392 = 645.41 A. Take k as 46 here. On a real job, read k for steel armour from Table 54.4. S = √(645.41² × 0.1) ÷ 46 = 4.44 mm². The armour is 22 mm², so it is justified as the cpc.

The extra length lets less fault current through. So it needs less armour than the 5.00 mm² worked on the plan length alone. A fault at the MDB end sees 2530 A. That needs 17.39 mm². That still passes.

At fault currents this high, an MCB clears well inside 0.1 s. So 17.39 mm² is a cautious figure. On a real job, the maker's let-through energy, I²t, gives the real need: k²S² must be at least that.

Carry Zs at DBL2, 0.392 Ω, to the circuit.

pages.name: Section A 3(h)
pages.task: From the worked example: the submain runs 20.0 m with its vertical runs. It drops 1.64 V three-phase, which is 0.95 V on a single-phase circuit. Assume the longest circuit is C7: the foyer's six LED fittings and the six walkway bollards. Its farthest bollard is about 20.8 m from DBL2 on plan. With 1.5 m up and 1.5 m down, it runs 23.8 m. It carries 1.21 A on 1.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. Its 1.21 A rests on assumed power factors. The singles drop 31 mV/A/m. A 6 A type C breaker protects it, because LED drivers draw a surge at switch-on. In conduit on a wall, Method B, two loaded cables carry 23 A. So 1.21 ≤ 6 ≤ 23. The bollards are outdoors, so a real design would pick a cable fit for that run. Here, assume the same singles run all the way. (h) Determine the total voltage drop from the intake to the farthest bollard, and state whether it complies.

Submain: 17.0 m on plan + 1.5 m up + 1.5 m down = 20.0 m

C7: 20.8 m on plan + 1.5 m up + 1.5 m down = 23.8 m

(g)Zs at DBL20.392 Ω

From the worked example: the submain runs 20.0 m with its vertical runs. It drops 1.64 V three-phase, which is 0.95 V on a single-phase circuit.

Assume the longest circuit is C7: the foyer's six LED fittings and the six walkway bollards. Its farthest bollard is about 20.8 m from DBL2 on plan. With 1.5 m up and 1.5 m down, it runs 23.8 m. It carries 1.21 A on 1.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. Its 1.21 A rests on assumed power factors. The singles drop 31 mV/A/m.

A 6 A type C breaker protects it, because LED drivers draw a surge at switch-on. In conduit on a wall, Method B, two loaded cables carry 23 A. So 1.21 ≤ 6 ≤ 23.

The bollards are outdoors, so a real design would pick a cable fit for that run. Here, assume the same singles run all the way.

Circuit drop = 31 × 1.21 × 23.8 ÷ 1000 = 0.89 V

Total = 0.95 + 0.89 = 1.84 V

1.84 V is 0.80% of 230 V, far under the 6.90 V allowed for lighting. So it complies.

Now check C1, the consultation bay. It is shorter but carries 4.89 A, also from assumed power factors. Over its 20.3 m it drops 3.08 V. From the intake that makes 4.03 V. That passes too. But C1, not C7, has the bigger drop.

Submain: 17.0 m on plan + 1.5 m up + 1.5 m down = 20.0 m

C7: 20.8 m on plan + 1.5 m up + 1.5 m down = 23.8 m

(g)Zs at DBL20.392 Ω
(h)Drop from the intake to C7's last bollard1.84 V

C7 runs 23.8 m. Its line and cpc are both 1.5 mm². Together they are 24.2 mΩ/m at 20 °C. Use the 1.28 multiplier.

R1+R2 = 24.2 × 1.28 × 23.8 ÷ 1000 = 0.737 Ω

Zs = 0.392 + 0.737 = 1.129 Ω

1.129 Ω is under the 6 A type C's maximum of 3.64 Ω. So it is acceptable. The least fault current is 230 × 0.95 ÷ 1.129 = 193.53 A. That is past 60 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s.

So k is 143. First, its minimum size.

Submain: 17.0 m on plan + 1.5 m up + 1.5 m down = 20.0 m

(g)Zs at DBL20.392 Ω
(h)Drop from the intake to C7's last bollard1.84 V
(i)Zs at C7's last bollard1.129 Ω

The cpc is copper and runs in the same conduit as the 90 °C thermosetting singles. So k is 143.

First, its minimum size.

Greatest fault current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 1.129 = 224.09 A

S = √(224.09² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 0.50 mm²

0.50 mm² is under the 1.5 mm² fitted, so the cpc satisfies the thermal constraints.

Check the DBL2 end too. A fault there sees 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.392 = 645.41 A. Then S = √(645.41² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 1.43 mm². That is a slim pass. Designers disagree about which end sets the thermal check. Checking both ends is the safe way.

At 645.41 A the breaker clears well inside 0.1 s, so the real margin is wider. On a real job, check the maker's let-through energy, I²t, against k²S².

Breaking capacity

The fault level is highest at the origin, at 4.6 kA. It falls along each cable. Take the breakers at the MDB and DBL2 as marked 6 kA for practice. That passes. Read the real Icn from each breaker.

The checklist, ticked

  • Every length of the run, not just the route on plan.20.0 m and 23.8 m.
  • Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz for each cable.8.22 ≤ 10 ≤ 37.84 A and 1.21 ≤ 6 ≤ 23 A.
  • Every voltage drop from the intake to the end.1.84 V against 6.90 V.
  • A three-phase drop turned into its single-phase share.1.64 V counted as 0.95 V.
  • Zs at the end against the device's maximum.0.392 Ω against 2.19 Ω, 1.129 Ω against 3.64 Ω.
  • The thermal constraints, with SWA armour as the cpc justified by calculation.Armour needs 17.39 mm² at the MDB end and 4.44 mm² at DBL2, of 22 mm². The cpc needs 1.43 mm² at the DBL2 end and 0.50 mm² at the far end, of 1.5 mm².
  • Breaking capacity at each device.6 kA against 4.6 kA.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why every length of the cable run must be included in the design calculations.
pages.why: A model answer: Every metre of cable adds resistance. It adds to the voltage drop, which is mV/A/m × Ib × length. It also adds to R1+R2, and so to Zs at the end of the circuit. A higher Zs lets less fault current flow, so the device may not open within the time allowed. The drop is judged from the intake to the end of the circuit, so the submain and every length before the circuit count too. A route measured on plan misses the runs up and down to boards and fittings, so the real cable is longer than the plan shows. Leave any length out and the design looks better than the installation will measure.

pages.name: Changed numbers
pages.task: A lighting circuit runs from a sub-board where Zs is 0.45 Ω. The submain adds 2.50 V to a single-phase circuit. The circuit is 1.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles with a 1.5 mm² cpc: 31 mV/A/m, 24.2 mΩ/m and the 1.28 multiplier. It carries 3.50 A on a 6 A type C breaker, whose maximum Zs is 3.64 Ω. Determine the longest the circuit can run and still meet both the 6.90 V limit and the maximum Zs.
pages.alt: A lighting circuit runs from a sub-board where Zs is 0.45 Ω. The submain adds 2.50 V to a single-phase circuit. The circuit is 1.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles with a 1.5 mm² cpc: 31 mV/A/m, 24.2 mΩ/m and the 1.28 multiplier. It carries 3.50 A on a 6 A type C breaker, whose maximum Zs is 3.64 Ω. Same method, new numbers. Give the length in metres. The drop allows (6.90 − 2.50) × 1000 ÷ (31 × 3.50) = 4400 ÷ 108.5 = 40.55, rounded down to 40.5 m Zs allows (3.64 − 0.45) × 1000 ÷ 30.976 = 102.98, rounded down to 102.9 m The drop sets it: 40.5 m At 3.50 A the drop runs out long before Zs does.

A lighting circuit runs from a sub-board where Zs is 0.45 Ω. The submain adds 2.50 V to a single-phase circuit. The circuit is 1.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles with a 1.5 mm² cpc: 31 mV/A/m, 24.2 mΩ/m and the 1.28 multiplier. It carries 3.50 A on a 6 A type C breaker, whose maximum Zs is 3.64 Ω.

Same method, new numbers. Give the length in metres.

The drop allows (6.90 − 2.50) × 1000 ÷ (31 × 3.50) = 4400 ÷ 108.5 = 40.55, rounded down to 40.5 m

Zs allows (3.64 − 0.45) × 1000 ÷ 30.976 = 102.98, rounded down to 102.9 m

The drop sets it: 40.5 m

At 3.50 A the drop runs out long before Zs does.
